title: Search Suggestions as You Type
statement:
A grocery delivery app suggests products while the user types. After each letter, the dropdown shows up to 3 products whose names start with what has been typed so far, picked as the 3 smallest names in alphabetical order.

Write def solution(products, search_word). products is a list of distinct product names. Return a list with one entry per letter of search_word: entry i is the list of up to 3 product names that start with search_word[:i + 1], sorted in plain Python string order (which is alphabetical for lowercase letters). If fewer than 3 match, list those; if none match, the entry is [].

examples.why: After m and mo, five names match and the 3 smallest are shown. From mou on, only mouse and mousepad match.
One product matches every prefix of its own name.
Fewer than 3 match te, and nothing matches tex.

constraints: only lowercase letters a to z; product names are distinct

think.q: How many lists do you return, and what can each one hold?
think.a: Exactly len(search_word) lists, one per typed letter. Each holds 0 to 3 names, sorted. Once a prefix matches nothing, every longer prefix also matches nothing, so the rest of the lists are [].

think.q: Products tea, teapot, toast, typed word tex. Write the three lists.
think.a: t: all three, sorted: tea, teapot, toast. te: tea, teapot. tex: nothing. So [["tea", "teapot", "toast"], ["tea", "teapot"], []].

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: For each prefix, filter all products with startswith, sort the matches and take 3. That repeats a full scan and a sort for every letter: O(L * n log n) for a word of length L.

A trie whose nodes remember their top 3 words. Sort the products first, then insert them in that order. On the way down, append the word to each node's list if it has fewer than 3. Because words arrive in sorted order, each node keeps exactly its 3 smallest matches. Typing a letter is then one step down the trie and a read of that node's list.

1. Sort products.
  2. For each product, walk from the root, creating nodes; at each node, if its top list has fewer than 3 names, append the product.
  3. Walk search_word from the root. For each letter, move to the child; if it is missing, stop moving and use [] for this and every later letter.
  4. Otherwise append a copy of the node's top list.

A prefix that matches nothing, followed by more letters (all later entries are [], even if a product starts with those later letters on their own). A product that is a prefix of another (tea before teapot). A search word longer than every product. Fewer than 3 matches. Products given unsorted.

hints: Each typed letter extends the prefix by one character. In a trie that is one step down from the previous node, not a new search.
Sort the products before you insert them. Then, at every node, the first 3 words that pass through are the 3 smallest.
Store a top list on each node and append while it has fewer than 3 words. When the typed word leaves the trie, the current and all later entries are [].
brute:
def solution(products, search_word):
    # For every prefix, scan and sort all matches: O(L * n log n).
    out = []
    for i in range(1, len(search_word) + 1):
        prefix = search_word[:i]
        matches = sorted(name for name in products if name.startswith(prefix))
        out.append(matches[:3])
    return out
explain:
Example 1: sorted products are mobile, moneypot, monitor, mouse, mousepad; the typed word is mouse.

  • Insert them in that order. The nodes for m and mo fill up with mobile, moneypot, monitor; mouse and mousepad arrive when those lists are full.
  • The node for mou gets mouse, then mousepad. So do mous and mouse.
  • Walking m, o, u, s, e reads [mobile, moneypot, monitor] twice, then [mouse, mousepad] three times.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and inserting costs O(total letters), with at most 3 names stored per node. Each typed letter is then one dict lookup. Another good answer skips the trie: sort the products and, for each prefix, use bisect_left to find the first name that is not smaller than the prefix, then check the next 3 names.
complexity: O(n log n + total letters) to build, O(L) to answer a word of length L; O(total letters) space
